title: Making capsule networks cope with hundreds of classes
paper_title: Using dynamic routing to extract intermediate features for developing scalable capsule networks
date_note: ICACCP 2019 (2nd Int. Conf. on Advanced Computational and Communication Paradigms), Gangtok, Sikkim, 25-28 Feb 2019 (from my knowledge of the venue; the PDF only shows the 2019 copyright line)
venue: 2nd International Conference on Advanced Computational and Communication Paradigms (ICACCP)
authors: B Mandal, Swarnendu Ghosh, R Sarkhel, N Das, M Nasipuri
summary: Capsule networks get slow and memory-hungry as the number of classes grows. We changed what their routing step produces, which cut training time and raised accuracy on 199-class handwritten Bangla characters.

body.p: Capsule networks are image classifiers that store each detected feature as a small list of numbers instead of a single value. They were shown to work well on ten-class problems such as digits, but they get slow and memory-hungry when the number of classes grows. We changed what the routing step of the network produces, so that the routing no longer depends on how many classes there are.

In an ordinary neural network, each unit outputs one number. A capsule outputs a vector, an arrow in a space of 8 or 16 dimensions. The length of the arrow says how likely it is that something is present, and its direction describes how it looks. A capsule network first builds many small primary capsules from convolutions. Then a step called dynamic routing lets these primary capsules vote for the final answer. The votes are weighed again and again during a single forward pass, and a vote counts more when it agrees with the combined answer.

In the original design the final layer holds one 16-dimensional capsule per class. That means the number of routing weights grows in direct proportion to the number of classes. When we tried the network on problems with more classes, it took a lot of time to train, and its accuracy dropped. Earlier work by others had reported the same loss of accuracy on more complicated data. With many classes there are many more relationships between capsules to check, and the network tends to overfit.

figure.alt: Diagram of the original capsule network: an image goes through a convolution, becomes primary capsules, is routed into one output capsule per class, and a decoder reconstructs the input.
figure.caption: The original design ends in one output capsule for every class, so the routing step grows with the number of classes.

body.p: We used dynamic routing for a different job. Instead of producing one capsule per class, the routing step produces a set of feature capsules. Each of them is still a 16-dimensional vector, but it stands for a learned feature, not for a class. The feature capsules are flattened and passed to an ordinary fully connected layer, which turns them into class scores.

Think of describing a person by a few traits instead of keeping a separate checklist for everyone you might meet. Samples can often be described with fewer features than there are classes, and the routing now depends only on the number of features. The decoder, which rebuilds the input image as a regulariser, works from the full set of feature capsules, with no masking.

figure.alt: Diagram of the proposed network: the same primary capsules are routed into a few feature capsules, which are flattened into a fully connected layer for the classes, with a decoder for reconstruction.
figure.caption: In the proposed network the routing output is a small set of feature capsules, and a fully connected layer maps them to the classes.

body.p: We tested on five handwritten data sets from the Indic scripts: Bangla, Devanagari and Telugu numerals (10 classes each), Bangla basic characters (50 classes) and Bangla compound characters (199 classes). We compared against the standard capsule network on a GTX 1080 Ti with 11 GB of memory. The number of feature capsules, N<sub>features</sub>, was the main setting we varied.

On the ten-class numerals there was not much change in accuracy (Table V). Training time per epoch (one pass over the training data) dropped, though. For Bangla numerals it went from 11.57 seconds with the standard network to 5.54 seconds with two feature capsules, and to 11.19 seconds with ten (Table VI).
The gains are larger on the bigger problems:

ul: Bangla basic characters (50 classes): accuracy rose from 90.6% to 93.23% with eight feature capsules (Table X), and the epoch time fell from 120.61 to 25.74 seconds (Table XI).
Bangla compound characters (199 classes): accuracy rose from 79.34% to 87.44% with six feature capsules (Table X), and the epoch time fell from 1,206.99 to 59.65 seconds (Table XI).

body.callout: With six feature capsules on the 199-class compound characters, accuracy went from 79.34% to 87.44% while training time per epoch fell from 1,206.99 to 59.65 seconds (Tables X and XI).

body.p: The paper's explanation is that the major speed-up comes from memory, not from faster arithmetic per sample. The standard network needed 2,057 MB per sample on the compound set, while ours needed between 667 and 801 MB, whichever number of feature capsules we used from 2 to 20 (Table VIII). The largest possible batch size grew from 16 to as many as 1,520 images (Table IX), which makes much better use of a GPU's parallel hardware.

We also compared our best results with other published methods. On compound characters we reached 87.44% against 86.64% for the best earlier method in our list, and on basic characters 93.23% against 92.15% (Table XII). We conclude that the network beats many other popular works on these Indic data sets.

On the numerals, we saw no real accuracy gain, only the time saving. The speed advantage also disappears when N<sub>features</sub> goes beyond the number of classes, so the number of feature capsules should stay below the number of classes. We chose the number of feature capsules for each data set, and we did not use a separate validation set: we kept the model with the best training performance and reported its test accuracy.

Because the decoder sees all feature capsules at once, the network can no longer produce a reconstruction of one specific class. We also have not yet studied how feature capsules relate to equivariance, the property that motivated capsules in the first place. The paper names both as directions for future work.
The practical result is that a character set with 199 classes took 59.65 seconds per epoch with six feature capsules, where the standard capsule network took 1,206.99 seconds (Table XI).
